pr_title: Fix config binding with records having collection constructor parameter

issue_context.title: In .Net 7 attempting to Get a configuration section using a type defined as a record will duplicate array values.
issue_context.body:
**Edited by @tarekgh** This issue claimed the problem is not occurring on .NET 6.0 which is not true. The comment https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/83803#issuecomment-1480482130 clarified that. In short, this issue is not a regression from .NET 6.0. Actually, .NET 7.0 behavior is not throwing. **End of @tarekgh edit** _This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/In-Net-7-attempting-to-Get-a-configurat/10304171)._ --- [severity:It bothers me. A fix would be nice] The behaviour has changed unexpectedly from how .Net 6.0 used to work. ``` /* Environment Variables "MonitorConfig__Services__0__Name": "Service A" "MonitorConfig__Services__0__Url": "http://localhost:5201/health", "MonitorConfig__Services__1__Name": "Service B", "MonitorConfig__Services__1__Url": "http://localhost:5202/health" */ /* defined Records types public record MonitorConfig(ServiceConfig[] Services = null); public record ServiceConfig(string Name, string Url); */ var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables(); var monitorConfig = builder.Configuration.GetSection("MonitorConfig").Get(); ``` monitorConfig will contain 4 ServiceConfig entries with duplicated instances of both ServiceA and ServceB declarations. The expectation should be two entries as defined by the environment variables. If I convert to use class types instead of record types, the behaviour works as expected. The use of records should be supported and work as it did for .Net 6.0 using the same code, as I should not have to go and rewrite records to as classes after porting to .Net 7. --- ### Original Comments #### Feedback Bot on 3/8/2023, 05:37 PM: (private comment, text removed) --- ### Original Solutions #### Chris Westermann solved on 3/9/2023, 05:05 AM, 0 votes:

I found that if I override the default constructor, then I get the behaviour I would expect

public record MonitorConfig(ServiceConfig[] Services)
{
public MonitorConfig()
: this((ServiceConfig[])null)
{ }
}

While this is a workaround, it seems odd I would need to do this since, conceptually, setting the default value of the positional parameter to null should produce the same behaviour and not cause the actual instance to have twice as many array entries as expected.
comments:
Without the workaround of adding a default public constructor, this code actually throws an exception in .NET 6.0 - but the original posted said it used to work. Here is the behaviors based on my experimentation:

| Runtime | Has default public constructor | Behavior |
|-|-|-|
| .NET 6.0 | Yes | Runs - creates two ServiceConfig elements |
| .NET 7.0 | Yes | Runs - creates two ServicConfig elements |
| .NET 6.0 | No | Runtime exception about lack of public constructor |
| .NET 7.0 | No | Runs - creates **four** ServiceConfig elements |

It looks like logic was added in .NET 7.0 to support non-default constructors where the parameters line up with properties (basically record types). But it's possible that there is a bug in there somewhere.
I transferred this over to the runtime repo because I think that is where the bug is.

The Issue here is during the binding to types (like record), we try to create instance of the type:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6246ce37ef665f5dc08b542a1ab092d90293eb62/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/src/ConfigurationBinder.cs#L385

`CreateInstance` finds out the type doesn't have the parameter-less constructor and then tries to do binding through the constructor having parameters. 

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6246ce37ef665f5dc08b542a1ab092d90293eb62/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/src/ConfigurationBinder.cs#L468

Will bind the configuration to the parameters and send call the constructor with the initialized parameters. The constructor will set the parameters values to the properties. 

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6246ce37ef665f5dc08b542a1ab092d90293eb62/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/src/ConfigurationBinder.cs#L471

After that will continue the binding process on the created object by going through binding its properties

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6246ce37ef665f5dc08b542a1ab092d90293eb62/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/src/ConfigurationBinder.cs#L408

This will cause binding again the property which was already set during the constructor initialization which will duplicate the entries inside the created list as the property is of type `Array`.

This is why when having a parameter-less constructor fix the issue because it will be used and will not do any config binding during creating the object (through CreateInstance).

@heldersousa-planetpayment What you are explaining regarding the class differs from the original issue at hand. The initial problem revolved around a property binding occurring twice in the configuration. Conversely, your concern pertains to the distinction between extending and mutating the original collection. In .NET 7.0, a [breaking change](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/extensions/7.0/config-bind-dictionary) was introduced, primarily addressing dictionaries but applicable to other collections like arrays. It's not clear why extending array values instead of overriding them might be perceived as unconventional. Both approaches have valid arguments, and I recall encountering scenarios where extending the collection was deemed necessary.

I largely concur with your assessment in this matter. Our current challenge revolves around resolving the binding issue with the record. As you rightly pointed out, tackling this issue to prevent the binding of properties twice should also effectively address the scenario you've outlined.

> I appreciate there may be cases where the example provided in [Binding config to dictionary extends values](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/extensions/7.0/config-bind-dictionary) makes sense

The example is streamlined to illustrate the behavior. In some cases, users create an object and bind it to multiple configuration sources, anticipating the aggregation of values from various configurations. I share your agreement that utilizing a record is not the intended scenario, and this is something we need to address by preventing the occurrence of double binding.
@bartkemps yes, this is why we still have the issue opened to track it.

Just ran into this issue. Unfortunately we can't mitigate the issue by providing another constructor that doesn't accept the config so we are somewhat stuck.

Edit: I actually found a workaround that makes the List itself private and exposes a ReadOnly version as a property.

> Edit: I actually found a workaround that makes the List itself private and exposes a ReadOnly version as a property.

@Blackclaws can you share the workaround? I'm curious about how it works. Wouldn't the second call fail when trying to add elements to the ReadOnly list?

review_comments: Is this just here for compatibility to make sure we still call the setters for types that have constructor parameters?

That is right. Look at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/06ac04f5a946a4db281405d616f89d8f44bb2d6b/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/tests/Common/ConfigurationBinderTests.TestClasses.cs#L170 as example that can break if we don't do that.
